filings.topic: TCP BBR vs CUBIC congestion control
filings.content:
TCP BBR vs CUBIC congestion control

CUBIC is a loss-based congestion control algorithm: it grows the congestion window until packet loss occurs, then backs off. BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time) is model-based: it measures bottleneck bandwidth and minimum RTT, then paces sends to operate at that point without filling buffers.

How CUBIC works

CUBIC increases the window using a cubic function of time since the last congestion event. On packet loss (or ECN marking), it reduces the window and enters congestion avoidance. Because it relies on loss as a signal, CUBIC tends to fill router buffers, which can raise queuing latency — especially on links with large buffers (bufferbloat).

How BBR works

BBR maintains a model of the network path: the maximum recent bandwidth (bw) and the minimum round-trip propagation time (min_rtt). It uses these to compute a target sending rate and paces packets accordingly. Instead of waiting for loss, BBR probes for more bandwidth and more headroom in controlled cycles, keeping the pipe full while minimizing queue buildup.

Practical differences

  • Latency: BBR typically keeps latency lower on buffer-bloated links because it avoids filling buffers; CUBIC can add significant queuing delay.
  • Congestion signal: CUBIC reacts to loss or ECN; BBR reacts to delivery rate and RTT measurements.
  • Short paths: CUBIC can perform well on short, high-bandwidth paths where loss is rare and buffers are small.
  • Fairness: BBR can be more aggressive than loss-based flows when sharing a bottleneck, which may affect fairness with CUBIC or Reno traffic.

In short: CUBIC fills the pipe until loss tells it to back off; BBR measures the pipe and paces to stay at the optimal operating point.

Tailscale ACLs: rules vs tags

An ACL rule defines which sources can reach which destinations and ports. A tag is an identity assigned to a device rather than a user, so tagged devices keep their access even when the person who set them up leaves.

Regular ACL rules

A regular rule maps a source (such as a user or group) to a destination and port. For example: group:admins can reach 10.0.0.5 on port 443. The access is tied to the user's identity.

Tags

A tag labels a device as a service identity instead of a person-owned node. Rules can reference tag:server as a source or destination. Because the tag belongs to the device, not a user, access persists across personnel changes.

Example

group:admins can reach tag:server on port 22 lets admins SSH into any device tagged server, regardless of which specific device holds the tag.

filings.content:
CAP theorem

The CAP theorem states that a distributed data store experiencing a network partition cannot simultaneously guarantee consistency and availability. During a partition, a system must choose: CP (consistency over availability, refusing writes until the partition heals) or AP (availability over consistency, continuing to serve reads and writes and reconciling later). When no partition exists, both consistency and availability can be provided, so the real design decision is how the system behaves during failures.

Consistency

Every read receives the most recent write or an error. All nodes see the same data at the same time.

Availability

Every request receives a non-error response, without guaranteeing that it reflects the most recent write.

Partition tolerance

The system continues to operate despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped or delayed between nodes. Partitions are unavoidable in distributed networks, so partition tolerance is not optional.

Practical implication

Because partitions cannot be prevented, architects choose CP or AP based on workload needs. Financial ledgers typically favor CP; social feeds and shopping carts often favor AP.

filings.content:
What is LLM quantization?

Quantization reduces the precision of model weights from 16 or 32 bits down to 8, 4, or fewer bits, making the model smaller and faster to compute with a small trade-off in accuracy.

Why GGUF enables faster inference

GGUF is a file format that stores quantized weights alongside a memory-mappable layout, allowing local inference engines to load and map weights directly into memory quickly without full deserialization.

Key benefits

  • Reduced model size and memory footprint
  • Faster inference on CPU and consumer hardware
  • Lower bandwidth and storage requirements
  • Minimal accuracy loss at appropriate quantization levels

Common quantization levels

  • Q8_0: 8-bit, near-original quality
  • Q4_K_M: 4-bit, good balance of size and quality
  • Q2_K: 2-bit, smallest size with noticeable quality loss

filings.content:
How Ada Nest Heartbeat Escalation Works

Each member node sends a heartbeat to the hub at a fixed interval, and the hub tracks how fresh each heartbeat is. If a member misses N consecutive beats, its state moves from healthy to stale, then to degraded; only if it stays degraded past the degraded window without recovering does the hub escalate by paging you.

State progression

  1. Healthy: heartbeats arrive within the expected interval.
  2. Stale: the member has missed N beats; the hub marks it stale but takes no further action.
  3. Degraded: the stale condition persists beyond the stale-to-degraded threshold.
  4. Page: the member remains degraded through the full degraded window without a recovering heartbeat, so the hub pages you.

What this prevents

A single missed beat or a brief Wi‑Fi flap never reaches your phone, because escalation requires the full sequence: missed beats → stale → degraded → window expiry without recovery. Temporary network hiccups that recover before the degraded window ends are absorbed silently.

Key parameters

  • Heartbeat interval: how often each member sends a beat.
  • N (missed beats): the count of consecutive misses that flips a member to stale.
  • Degraded window: the time the hub waits after degradation before paging.

Created lesson-465f4d854725 (Tailscale ACL tags vs rules) — new lesson explaining how ACL rules map users/groups to destinations while tags provide device-level identity for infrastructure access that outlives individual users.

filings.content:
Tailscale ACL rules vs tags

An ACL rule defines which sources can reach which destinations and ports in your tailnet. A tag is a device-level identity that lets you write rules based on the machine rather than the person who owns it.

A regular ACL rule maps users or groups to destinations: for example, group:admins can reach 10.0.0.5 on port 22. Access follows the user, so if that person leaves the organization, their devices lose access unless another rule covers them.

A tag (like tag:server) is attached to a device itself, not to a user. Tagged devices are owned by the tailnet, not by a person, so access persists even when users leave. You write rules such as group:admins can reach tag:server on port 22 — the tag becomes the node identity in the rule.

Use tags for infrastructure (servers, databases, CI runners) where access should outlive individual users. Use regular user/group rules for people-based access. Tags require the device to be authorized with the tag key, and only authorized users can apply tags during device authorization.

filings.content:
CAP theorem

The CAP theorem states that a distributed data store experiencing a network partition cannot simultaneously guarantee consistency and availability — it must choose one. During a partition, a system can be CP (consistent but unavailable: it refuses writes until the partition heals) or AP (available but not immediately consistent: it keeps serving reads and writes, reconciling state later). When no partition exists, both consistency and availability can be provided, so the real engineering decision is how the system behaves during failures.

Trade-offs

  • CP: prioritises consistency; nodes may reject requests during a partition to avoid serving stale data.
  • AP: prioritises availability; nodes keep responding, accepting temporary inconsistency that must be resolved after the partition ends.

CAP applies only while a network partition is active; normal operation is not constrained by the theorem.

clawbot.final_text: Created lesson `lesson-ab249dd03191` ("Ada LLM quantization GGUF") covering LLM quantization and GGUF memory-mapped inference.

filings.content:
What is LLM quantization and why GGUF speeds up inference

Quantization reduces the precision of model weights from 16 or 32 bits down to 8, 4, or fewer bits, making the model smaller and faster to compute at a small cost in accuracy. GGUF is a file format that stores quantized weights with a memory-mappable layout, enabling fast local inference.

How quantization works

LLM weights are typically stored as floating-point numbers (FP16 or FP32). Quantization maps these values to a smaller set of discrete levels using lower-precision integers such as INT8 or INT4. The model's size shrinks proportionally, memory bandwidth drops, and arithmetic becomes cheaper, while output quality usually degrades only slightly.

Why GGUF is faster for local inference

GGUF packages quantized weights alongside metadata in a layout designed for memory mapping (mmap). The operating system can load weight pages on demand instead of reading the whole file into RAM, reducing startup time and memory pressure. This makes GGUF well suited for running quantized LLMs on consumer hardware.

Trade-offs

  • Lower bit widths reduce model size and increase inference speed.
  • Aggressive quantization can lose nuance and reduce accuracy on difficult tasks.
  • GGUF is optimized for CPU/local inference, not for distributed training.

How Ada Nest heartbeat escalation works

Each member node sends a heartbeat to the hub at a fixed interval, and the hub tracks how fresh each heartbeat is. A page is only triggered after a member misses N consecutive heartbeats, enters a stale state, then passes through a degraded window without recovering — so a single missed beat or brief network flap never reaches your phone.

Heartbeat flow

  1. The hub expects a heartbeat from each member every interval.
  2. If a member misses a beat, its state becomes stale.
  3. If the member stays stale past the degraded window without sending a new heartbeat, the hub escalates.
  4. Escalation pages the on-call contact.

What prevents false pages

  • A single missed beat only marks the member stale — no page.
  • A brief network flap that recovers within the degraded window returns the member to healthy without escalation.
  • Only sustained silence across N beats plus the full degraded window triggers a page.

Tailscale ACLs: tags versus regular rules

A Tailscale ACL rule defines which sources can reach which destinations and ports; a tag is a device-level identity that replaces user ownership so access survives user departures.

Regular ACL rules are written in terms of users and groups: group:admins can reach user:alice on port 443. When a user leaves the organization, their devices and any rules referencing them lose effect.

filings.content:
CAP theorem

The CAP theorem states that a distributed data store cannot simultaneously guarantee consistency, availability, and partition tolerance. When a network partition occurs, the system must choose between consistency and availability.

Consistency

Every read receives the most recent write or an error. All nodes see the same data at the same time.

Availability

Every request receives a response (success or failure), without guarantee that it reflects the most recent write.

Partition tolerance

The system continues to operate despite messages being dropped or delayed between nodes.

CP vs AP during a partition

  • CP (Consistent and Partition tolerant): The system refuses writes or returns errors to preserve consistency. Availability is sacrificed.
  • AP (Available and Partition tolerant): The system keeps serving requests and reconciles differences later. Consistency is sacrificed temporarily.

When there is no partition, a system can provide both consistency and availability. The CAP theorem therefore forces a trade-off only during network failures; the engineering decision is which property to prioritize when partitions happen.

clawbot.final_text: Created lesson-b5b147e7d64c (topic: "LLM quantization GGUF format") with intro-level content explaining LLM quantization, GGUF memory-mapped layout, and trade-offs; status open, next review 2026-10-31.

filings.content:
LLM Quantization and GGUF Format

Quantization reduces the precision of LLM model weights from 16 or 32 bits down to 8, 4, or fewer bits, making the model smaller and faster to compute at a small cost in accuracy. GGUF is a file format that stores quantized weights with a memory-mappable layout, enabling fast local inference.

How Quantization Works

LLM weights are typically stored as floating-point numbers (FP16 or FP32). Quantization maps these to lower-precision representations such as INT8 or INT4. Each weight tensor is scaled so the reduced range still captures the distribution of the original values. The result is a smaller model file that requires less memory bandwidth and can run on consumer hardware.

Why GGUF Is Faster

GGUF stores quantized weights alongside metadata in a single file designed for memory mapping (mmap). The operating system can map file pages directly into the process address space, so only the tensors needed for the current computation are loaded. This avoids full-model loading and reduces startup time. GGUF also carries quantization metadata such as block scales and offsets, allowing the inference engine to dequantize on the fly during matrix multiplication.

Trade-offs

  • Lower precision can slightly reduce model accuracy, especially at 4-bit or below.
  • Quantized models need inference engines that support the specific quantization type.
  • GGUF is optimized for local CPU inference and may not be the best choice for GPU training or serving.

Escalation stages
